24:2.text: But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.

provenance.other: “we will not have this man to reign over us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 19:14, and “would not that I should reign over them” in exactly one, Luke 19:27. The Book of Mormon's clause, 'they would not that he should be their king', is Luke 19:27's construction with 'be their king' for 'reign over them' — near enough to be recognized, not near enough to be a quotation.
provenance.significance: The parable of the pounds is the KJV's one story of subjects who refuse a king they already have: a nobleman goes into a far country to receive a kingdom, his citizens send after him to say they will not have him reign over them, and when he returns his last order is that those enemies be brought and slain before him. Alma 24 sets the same refusal in motion and then declines its ending. The rebels take up arms against a king who will not defend himself, and instead of the enemies being slain before him, his people are slain in front of them without resistance. Luke 19's outcome is the outcome the chapter is written to refuse — which is also why the parable's other half, the servant who hid what he was given in a napkin, has already been used at Mosiah 9:2 without this half.

24:2.note: 'They began to rebel against their king, insomuch that they would not that he should be their king.' Two KJV singletons say this and both are in the parable of the pounds, twelve verses apart: the citizens' message at Luke 19:14 and the nobleman's judgment on them at 19:27. The Book of Mormon paraphrases rather than quotes, which is why this is moderate — 'would not that he should be their king' keeps Luke's syntax and changes his verb. Mosiah 9:2 has already drawn on the same parable for a different purpose, so the passage is available to the book; what is new here is the citizens' refusal rather than the servant's excuse. The 1830 reads 'insomuch that' twice in one sentence, which the later editions leave standing.

24:13.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 7:14, and “made them white in the blood” in exactly one, the same verse. 'Stain' is a rare KJV word — three verses, Job 3:5, Isaiah 23:9 and Isaiah 63:3 — and only Isaiah 63:3 stains anything with blood: 'their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment', spoken by the treader of the winepress.
provenance.significance: Alma 5:21 and 13:11 have already used Revelation 7:14 in its own terms, of garments made white in the blood of the Lamb. Alma 24:13 changes the object, and the change is the chapter's whole argument: it is not robes but swords that are washed, and not white but bright. A garment washed in blood is a paradox one can absorb as metaphor; a murder weapon washed clean in the blood of the murdered God is the same paradox made intolerable, and the speech uses it to argue that the cleaning cannot be repeated. The Isaiah 63 figure sits underneath — the one KJV passage where blood stains rather than whitens — so that the two directions blood can run in scripture are set against each other across two verses of one sermon.

24:13.note: 'If we should stain our swords again, they can no more be washed bright through the blood of the Son of our great God, which shall be shed for the atonement of our sins.' The washing-in-blood figure is Revelation 7:14's, a verse with two phrases that occur nowhere else in the KJV, and it has been used twice already in this book of garments (5:21, 13:11). This is not that formula recurring. The object has moved from what a convert wears to what he killed with, and the sermon's practical conclusion — bury the swords, they cannot be cleaned twice — depends entirely on the transfer. Note also the transposed adjective: Revelation's robes are made white, and these swords are made bright, which is what a sword and not a robe can be.

24:17.text: Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.

provenance.other: “man's blood” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 9:6 and Acts 5:28, and “whoso sheddeth man's blood” in exactly one, Genesis 9:6. The Book of Mormon's phrase, 'the shedding of man's blood', is Genesis 9:6's noun in Hebrews 9:22's construction — “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22, 'without shedding of blood is no remission', which this book has adjudicated at Alma 34:13.
provenance.significance: Genesis 9:6 is the King James Bible's foundational prohibition of homicide, and its second half is the reason: 'for in the image of God made he man.' That doctrine is what Aaron read to this king's father two chapters earlier — Alma 22:12, 'how God created man after his own image' — and the covenant sworn here is the first half of the same verse. The catalogue's finding is the arc: the Lamanite conversion begins with Genesis 1:27 read to a king and ends with Genesis 9:6 enacted by his son's people, which is the order the KJV itself puts them in and the logic Genesis 9:6 itself supplies. Note what the burial does to the verse's sanction, though. Genesis 9:6 answers bloodshed with bloodshed, 'by man shall his blood be shed'; these people bury the means of the answer and then let their own blood be shed at 24:21-22 without returning it.

24:17.note: 'They took their swords, and all the weapons which were used for the shedding of man's blood, and they did bury them up deep in the earth.' 'Man's blood' is a KJV phrase of two verses and the shedding of it is Genesis 9:6's, the covenant with Noah that grounds the prohibition of murder in the image of God. The phrase carries through into 24:18, where the covenant is spelled out — 'that they never use weapons again for the shedding of man's blood' — so the link is adjudicated here at its first occurrence. The construction 'the shedding of' is Hebrews 9:22's rather than Genesis's, which is worth recording because 24:13 has just made the blood of the Son the thing that cleans the swords, and Hebrews 9:22 is the verse that makes shed blood the condition of remission.

24:18.text: Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.

provenance.other: “working with his hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:28, and “to give to him that needeth” occurs in exactly one, the same verse. Paul's other statements about manual labour — 1 Corinthians 4:12, 1 Thessalonians 4:11, 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12 — have the working but not the giving, and it is the giving that Alma 24:18 has.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 4:28 is a single sentence containing a three-step exchange: stop taking, work with your hands, so that you have something to give. Alma 24:18 has the same three steps in the same order — 'rather than to take away from a brother, they would give unto him; and rather than to spend their days in idleness, they would labor abundantly with their hands' — and reproduces Paul's 'but rather' construction twice over. What the Book of Mormon adds is the step before: 'rather than to shed the blood of their brethren, they would give up their own lives.' Read Ephesians 4:28 back into the verse and the covenant is Paul's rule for a converted thief extended upward one degree, from property to life, with the same grammar carrying both. That is a strong argument for the borrowing being deliberate rather than incidental: the shape 'rather than X, they would Y' is Paul's, and the Book of Mormon runs it three times.

24:18.note: 'Rather than to take away from a brother, they would give unto him; and rather than to spend their days in idleness, they would labor abundantly with theit their hands.' Ephesians 4:28 is the only KJV verse that joins renounced theft, manual labour and giving to the needy, and it contributes two phrases that occur nowhere else in the Bible. The Book of Mormon's version keeps Paul's antithetical 'but rather' and his sequence while replacing his imperative with a covenant in the third person. The 1830 reading preserves a compositor's dittography, 'with theit their hands', which the later editions silently repair; the doubled word is a printing accident and carries no argument, but it is the running text.

24:19.text: Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.

provenance.other: The two distinctive phrases of the source are both KJV singletons — “resisted unto blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “striving against sin” occurs in exactly one, both Hebrews 12:4 — but the Book of Mormon reproduces neither of them. The contact is the proposition, not the wording: dying rather than sinning.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 12:4 is a reproach. Its readers have not yet paid for their resistance to sin with their lives, and the writer says so to shame them into endurance. Alma 24:19 reports a people who have. The reproach and the report are the two halves of one idea, and the Book of Mormon's sentence is what Hebrews 12:4 describes as not having happened yet — which is worth noticing because the verse is immediately followed in Hebrews by the discipline of sons, and Alma 24 is a chapter in which fathers' sins are what the children are being spared.

24:19.note: 'They were firm, and would suffer even unto death, rather than to commit sin.' Hebrews 12:4 is the King James Bible's one verse that puts resistance unto blood and striving against sin in a single clause, which is exactly the trade Alma 24:19 says these converts made. No phrase is reproduced, so this is registered as an echo and kjvSpecific is 'uncertain': 'suffer unto death' and 'commit sin' are ordinary English and Revelation 2:10's 'be thou faithful unto death' is an equally available background.
24:19.whyNot: There is no verbal contact at all beyond commonplaces. A reader may fairly say that a narrator summarizing a martyrdom would write this sentence with no New Testament verse in view, and that Hebrews 12:4 has been selected after the fact because it is memorable.

24:23.text: Ye shall observe to do therefore as the LORD your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

provenance.other: “turn aside to the right hand or to the left” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 5:32 — ten continuous words. The KJV's other right-hand-or-left formulas differ in the joint: Deuteronomy 17:11 and 17:20 and 28:14 and Joshua 1:7 and 23:6 all read 'to the right hand, or to the left' but attach it to other verbs ('decline', 'turn not', 'depart'). Only Deuteronomy 5:32 has 'turn aside to'.
provenance.significance: The ten words are the closing sentence of the KJV's second giving of the Ten Commandments — Deuteronomy 5 ends the Decalogue with 'ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left', meaning do not deviate from what you were commanded — and the sixth of those commandments, at Deuteronomy 5:17, is the one this people has covenanted to keep. Alma 23:3 had their king proclaim that Decalogue; Alma 24:17 had them bury the means of breaking it; and here, with swords coming down on them, the KJV's idiom for exact obedience becomes a description of their bodies. They do not turn aside to the right hand or to the left because they will not move at all. That is metalepsis in Hays's sense: the phrase is dead metaphor in Deuteronomy and is reanimated by being taken literally, and the reader who recovers Deuteronomy 5 finds the commandment the whole scene is about sitting fifteen verses above it.

24:23.note: 'Their brethren would not flee from the sword, neither would they turn aside to the right hand or to the left, but that they would lay down and perish, and praised God even in the very act of perishing under the sword.' A ten-word run reproducing a KJV singleton exactly, and the machine stream found it — the longest run in the chapter by a wide margin. It is catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the run and of the source being identifiable beyond dispute, while falling below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and forming no part of his list. The idiom is Deuteronomy's figure for not deviating from a commandment, and it is used here of men physically refusing to dodge. The 1830's 'they would lay down and perish' is the first edition's; 1920 corrects 'lay' to 'lie', which tidies the grammar and slightly weakens the picture of men going down deliberately. 'In the very act' is John 8:4's phrase, the KJV's only occurrence, and it belongs there to a woman taken in adultery — the wording of a sin caught in progress, given here to men caught in the act of dying well.

24:30.text: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

provenance.route: Hebrews 6:4-6, with 2 Peter 2:20-21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “once enlightened” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:4, and “fall away” occurs in exactly two, Hebrews 6:6 and Luke 8:13. The closing clause has a second source: 2 Peter 2:20-21 is the KJV's statement that for those who have known the way of righteousness and turned back, 'the latter end is worse with them than the beginning' and 'it had been better for them not to have known'. “worse than the first” occurs in three KJV verses, of which Matthew 12:45 and Luke 11:26 are the returning unclean spirit — 'the last state of that man is worse than the first'.
provenance.significance: Mormon's editorial conclusion is assembled from the two New Testament passages on apostasy, and it takes one clause from each. Hebrews 6 supplies the enlightenment and the falling away; 2 Peter 2 supplies the comparison with never having known. The reason this matters for the chapter is that the conclusion is being drawn about the Amalekites and Amulonites, who are Nephite dissenters — men who had the knowledge and left it — and set against Lamanites who never had it. That is precisely the distinction Hebrews 6:4-6 and 2 Peter 2:20-21 exist to make, and the verse borrows both of them to make it. Note the one thing it does not borrow: Hebrews 6:6's conclusion that such people are impossible to renew, which the chapter has just disproved at 24:24-27, where a thousand of the attackers repent on the spot.

24:30.note: 'After a people has been once enlightened by the spirit of God, and hath had great knowledge of things pertaining to righteousness, and then have fallen away into sin and transgression, they become more hardened, and thus their estate becometh worse than as though they had never known these things.' Two KJV rarities anchor it: 'once enlightened' occurs only at Hebrews 6:4, and 'fall away' in this sense only at Hebrews 6:6. The final clause moves to the other classic apostasy passage — 2 Peter 2:20-21, better not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known and turned — with the comparative of Matthew 12:45's returning spirit, 'worse than the first', behind the wording of 'worse than as though they had never known'. What makes the composite worth stating rather than assuming is that the Book of Mormon takes the diagnosis from Hebrews and declines Hebrews' verdict, which the chapter's own narrative has just contradicted.
